title: Researching teacher education practices from within: Towards a pedagogy of teacher educators' professionalism
text_snippet: Researching teacher education practices from within: Towards a pedagogy of teacher educators' professionalism Abstract This paper aims at sharing possibilities for pedagogizing the professionalism of teacher educators working from within institutional contexts and whose challenging experiences are less represented in the published literature. Professionalism of university-based teacher educators has attracted scholarly interest in the Global North country and cross-country contexts. Notions such as becoming and pedagogies of enactment are some of the useful concepts developed and mobilized to understand teacher educators' professionalism in such contexts. These constructs are employed in this study within the frameworks of the experiences of a teacher educator who does research in a less-represented teacher education community in Eritrea. This article is based on qualitative data sets generated from a self-study research on embedding reflective teaching practices among a group of experienced teachers during the implementation of a teacher education program. Data from a self-reflective journal entries, post-lesson debriefs, & focused discussions with groups of critical friends were employed while analyzing teaching milestones and turning points. title: Navigating higher education in Hungary: An interpretative phenomenological analysis of students with ADHD's learning experiences
text_snippet: Navigating higher education in Hungary: An interpretative phenomenological analysis of students with ADHD's learning experiences Abstract Only a few qualitative studies focus on the learning experience of students with ADHD in higher education, particularly from a student-centred perspective and within Central and Eastern European contexts. This study aims to present an overview of the academic experience of students with ADHD in Hungarian higher education from a student perspective. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 students with ADHD. In-depth data analysis was conducted using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). Five constructs were identified: 1) Reflection on the Self, 2) Academic Environment, 3) Social and Interpersonal Experiences, 4) Institutional Barriers and Support, and 5) Disorganised Life. The findings reveal students' complex self-perception, often accompanied by feelings of being behind and low self-esteem, but also show growth through self-awareness and coping strategies. While academic experiences were generally positive, highlighting a sense of freedom and engaging learning environments, students reported challenges in social and daily life. title: Teacher status in Kazakhstan: A narrative review
text_snippet: Teacher status in Kazakhstan: A narrative review Abstract The social status of teachers in Kazakhstan has undergone a considerable transformation, shifting from the symbolic prestige associated with the Soviet era to contemporary challenges linked to low remuneration, feminisation, and declining societal recognition. This narrative literature review synthesises findings from 11 peer-reviewed studies that examine both historical and present-day dynamics of teacher status and professionalisation. The review identifies four key themes: (1) the coexistence of Soviet-era prestige with bureaucratic control and constrained professional autonomy; (2) the persistent influence of economic and regional inequalities on teachers' current status, despite legislative efforts such as the Law on the Status of a Teacher (2019); (3) the mixed effects of professionalisation initiatives, including teacher education reforms and attestation, which aim to strengthen professional identity yet often manifest as administrative and bureaucratic demands; and (4) Kazakhstan's gradual harmonization with international standards alongside continuing systemic constraints. title: Discourses and alternatives of quality culture in higher education
text_snippet: Discourses and alternatives of quality culture in higher education Abstract This paper examines how quality culture has been discursively constructed in higher education scholarship and policy, and develops an alternative conceptualization grounded in academic values rather than governance imperatives. Quality culture has become a central reference point in higher education, frequently positioned as a bridge between compliance-oriented quality assurance and enhancement-focused approaches. Despite its collegial rhetoric, the concept is embedded in wider socio-political rationalities that shape how institutions understand and enact quality. Drawing on Torraco's (2005) integrative review Grant and Booth's (2009) typology, the paper conducts a critical review of foundational, empirical, and policy-oriented scholarship on quality culture. It identifies three dominant framings of neoliberalism: quality culture, situated in accountability and efficiency; managerialism, which appropriates collegial language to advance organizational control; and global competition, which positions it as a mechanism for rankings and reputation. title: Teachers' perceptions of essay assessment and score variation under the Hungarian school-leaving examination rubric: An exploratory study
text_snippet: Teachers' perceptions of essay assessment and score variation under the Hungarian school-leaving examination rubric: An exploratory study Abstract This study examines how Hungarian language and literature teachers perceive essay assessment and how much score variation emerges when the official rubric of the intermediate-level Hungarian school-leaving examination is applied to a single script. The article combines two exploratory components. First, questionnaire data from 140 practising teachers were analysed to map everyday assessment practices, perceived difficulties, and views of the official scoring guide. Second, a single-script rating study examined how 40 teachers scored the same analytical essay with the official rubric. The survey results indicate that classroom writing assessment remains strongly product-oriented and is widely experienced as difficult because of its time demands, large class sizes, lack of time, and uncertainty surrounding assessment criteria. Respondents also viewed the official guide as only partly clear, especially in the domains of content, structure, and linguistic quality. The rating study showed substantial score dispersion in these same high-inference dimensions, whereas spelling and presentation varied less across raters. title: Intimate partner abuse and academics: The chain-mediating effect of alexithymia and self-esteem
text_snippet: Intimate partner abuse and academics: The chain-mediating effect of alexithymia and self-esteem Abstract The paper examines a serial mediation model in which alexithymia and self-esteem sequentially meditate the relationship between technology-facilitated abuse in relationships and academic engagement. The usage of digital and telecommunication technologies to manipulate and mistreat intimate partners are on the rise especially among adolescents. Commonly known as Technology-facilitated abuse (TFA) in relationships, it has potential implications for emotional functioning, self-worth and academic outcomes. However, the parallel and sequential pathway through which TFA impacts academic engagement (AE) remains completely understudied via alexithymia (A, mediator-1) and self-esteem (SE, mediator-2). By using a cross-sectional exploratory research design, data was collected from 412 students in higher education institutes across seven states in India using non-probability sampling technique. Four standardized measures assessed the interconnectedness of the variables. title: Creating a culture of academic freedom through international partnership: Insights from a European Universities Alliance
text_snippet: Creating a culture of academic freedom through international partnership: Insights from a European Universities Alliance Abstract This article analyzes elements for the creation of a culture of academic freedom within a European Universities Alliance (EUA), CHARM-EU. Set against the backdrop of global declines in academic freedom, this research presents evidence collected in Hungary, a country that has been referred to as a critical case in terms of democratic backsliding. The study explores interviews with faculty engaged with an EUA from a traditional university in Hungary through a phenomenographic method that organizes outcome spaces by gathering categories of description that result from the aggregation of units of meaning. The outcome spaces in this article are constructed according to guidelines devised by the European University Association for the promotion of academic freedom. Findings present specific dimensions and themes in which pedagogical practice in CHARM-EU's Master's in Global Challenges for Sustainability converge with the groundings of academic freedom. Discussion resorts to the concepts of pedagogical device and pedagogical discourse. In conclusion, international partnerships are deemed able to expand views on the political dimension of pedagogical innovation in higher education

title: Tenure-line faculty and the shifting structure of academic freedom in American public research-intensive universities
text_snippet: Tenure-line faculty and the shifting structure of academic freedom in American public research-intensive universities Abstract Universities have long been heralded as bastions of open inquiry and democratic discourse, yet their institutional autonomy and faculty members' academic freedom are increasingly imperilled. Rising political polarisation, shifting funding landscapes, and the erosion of traditional faculty protections have reshaped the contours of institutional autonomy and academic freedom across public research-intensive universities in the United States. This study examines how institutional size, financial resources, and federal- and state-level politics may have influenced the proportion of tenure-line faculty in the third year of the Obama (2014), Trump (2018), and Biden (2023) administrations. Drawing on IPEDS data for R1 and R2 public institutions, we first chart descriptive trends in enrollment, funding, and tenure-line faculty composition. We then employ bivariate correlations to explore linear associations and multivariate OLS regressions to isolate the unique effects of (under)graduate enrollment, state appropriations, federal grants, and political context (federal party affiliation and state trifecta control). title: Analysis of students' misconceptions about physical and chemical changes at the lower secondary level
text_snippet: Analysis of students' misconceptions about physical and chemical changes at the lower secondary level Abstract Misconceptions, i.e. students' erroneous ideas, represent a long-term problem in the teaching of science. Their existence has a negative impact on the process of acquiring scientific knowledge and prevents the creation of a correct conceptual framework. Students' alternative ideas prevent proper learning and understanding of phenomena. Students find concepts and phenomena in chemistry particularly difficult because they are hard to imagine and therefore understand abstract concepts. This study investigates misconceptions related to physical and chemical changes among students in grades 7 to 9 attending elementary schools where the language of instruction is either Slovak or Hungarian. Specifically, it aims to compare the occurrence and nature of these misconceptions between Slovak-speaking and Hungarian-speaking students, and to determine whether the language of instruction influences students' understanding of scientific concepts. The data collection instrument as a diagnostic test consisting of tasks of varying difficulty. title: The relationship between academic freedom and government policy effectiveness in Hungarian higher education after 1990
text_snippet: The relationship between academic freedom and government policy effectiveness in Hungarian higher education after 1990 Abstract Background and purpose This paper examines the evolution of academic freedom in Hungary from the political regime change of 1990 to the present, based on an analysis of higher education legislation. It aims to assess the extent to which changes in academic freedom correlate with the performance of the Hungarian government and broader autocratization processes. Theoretical framework The analysis builds on the findings of Lyer et al. (2023), which suggest that the decline of university autonomy is associated with wider political trends, particularly autocratization and political polarization. Accordingly, the central hypothesis is that academic freedom in Hungarian higher education co-moves with the degree of governmental autocratization. Methods The study applies a legal–institutional analysis of the main higher education acts (1993, 2005, 2011) and their major amendments (1996, 2015, 2021, 2022). On this basis, a composite indicator of academic freedom in Hungary is constructed and compared over time with the Government Watch Index (GWI). title: International students' belonging, acculturation, and integration at the University of Debrecen
text_snippet: International students' belonging, acculturation, and integration at the University of Debrecen Abstract Understanding international students' experiences is essential for supporting their adaptation and integration within host institutions. Despite Hungary's growing role as an emerging higher education destination, limited research has examined how international students navigate belonging, acculturation, and integration at a large university in Northeastern Hungary. This qualitative study explores these processes through semi-structured interviews with 21 international students enrolled in the university of Debrecen. Using thematic analysis, the study identifies three interconnected dimensions shaping students' experiences: the mismatch between pre-arrival expectations and everyday realities, the cultural and structural differences encountered in daily life, and the strategies students employ to integrate into the host environment. The findings highlight the importance of language accessibility, campus–city dynamics, and institutional support in shaping students' sense of belonging and sociocultural adjustment. title: Preservice mathematics teachers' confidence in teaching algebra: A scale adaptation study
text_snippet: Preservice mathematics teachers' confidence in teaching algebra: A scale adaptation study Abstract This study aimed to adapt the scale developed by Day and Hurrell (2013) and later adopted by Lau (2021) into Turkish and to assess middle school mathematics teacher candidates' confidence in teaching algebra. We also examined the validity and reliability of the scale and evaluated the candidates' confidence levels. A total of 267 senior preservice mathematics teachers from nineteen universities participated in the study. We collected the data using a nine-item Likert-type questionnaire. During the adaptation process, we translated the scale into Turkish, obtained expert feedback from two mathematics education specialists, revised the items based on their suggestions, and conducted a back-translation through another expert to ensure linguistic accuracy. We performed confirmatory factor analysis, which supported the proposed factor structure and provided evidence of satisfactory psychometric properties, including adequate convergent validity and high internal consistency. title: Academic freedom: Discourses in Europe
text_snippet: Academic freedom: Discourses in Europe Abstract This introductory article aims to underscore that the discussion about “academic freedom” – its benefits, its limitations and exposition to threats – is not a recent issue in wake of discussions on the consequences of digitalization, artificial intelligence, the changing role of higher education within a knowledge-based society, new geo-political tensions, etc. Rather, it is based on the conviction, that the recent analyses can be better understood, if they are reflected in the context of traditional notions and in the context of controversial interpretations in the decades preceding the recent discussions.

title: Cooperation between family and school as a key factor in the inclusion and success of pupils with autism spectrum disorders
text_snippet: Cooperation between family and school as a key factor in the inclusion and success of pupils with autism spectrum disorders Abstract The study aimed to examine parents' experiences of cooperation with schools and to identify the key factors influencing the quality of communication and the effectiveness of support for pupils with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Effective collaboration between family and school is essential for fostering the educational and social development of pupils with ASD. Meaningful parental involvement, transparent communication, and individualised learning approaches are central components of inclusive education. A qualitative research design was applied, using semi-structured interviews with four Slovak parents of children aged 12–15 years diagnosed with ASD. Given the small sample size, the study is presented as a pilot investigation, focusing on an in-depth analysis of a specific participant group rather than producing generalisable conclusions. Interviews were transcribed and analysed through content analysis to identify recurring categories and themes related to school–family cooperation. title: Recruitment, retention and replacement challenges in rural KwaZulu-Natal schools, South Africa: A systematic review
text_snippet: Recruitment, retention and replacement challenges in rural KwaZulu-Natal schools, South Africa: A systematic review Abstract Teacher shortages pose a critical threat to international education systems, negatively affecting the delivery of quality education and equitable learning opportunities. This crisis is particularly evident in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, where it worsens existing inequalities and hampers educational progress. This study employed a systematic literature review to examine the recruitment, retention, and replacement challenges faced by rural schools in KwaZulu-Natal. Secondary data were collected from databases such as Google Scholar and JSTOR, using defined inclusion criteria and a specified time frame, and analysed through thematic synthesis to explore teachers', administrators', and education stakeholders' experiences and strategies. The findings indicate that systemic factors-such as demographic changes, socioeconomic disparities and institutional challenges-play a role in the shortage of teachers. The study shows that specific structural, socioeconomic and organisational factors, including poor housing, limited access to services, heavy workloads and inconsistent hiring processes, drive teacher shortages in rural KwaZulu-Natal. title: Motivations and narratives in STEM learning: Perspectives from Filipino secondary learners
text_snippet: Motivations and narratives in STEM learning: Perspectives from Filipino secondary learners Abstract The underperformance of Filipino students in international assessments such as PISA and TIMSS highlights persistent challenges in STEM education and underscores the need to understand the factors that influence students' participation in STEM pathways. This qualitative case study investigated the factors influencing senior high school students' decisions to pursue the STEM strand and explored how their experiences shape their persistence in this pathway. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with 14 purposively selected Grade 12 STEM students from a public high school. The qualitative information was analyzed using Yin's five-phase analytical framework. The analysis revealed that students' choice of the STEM strand is shaped by two broad factors: external influences and personal and internal drivers. The study also found that experiential engagement in STEM activities and motivational drivers strengthen students' commitment and persistence in the strand, while also described how they navigated academic challenges and derived meaningful learning outcomes from their experiences. title: Assessing inclusiveness in higher education: Changes in the entry requirements and the approval process of equity measures for disadvantaged students in Hungary
text_snippet: Assessing inclusiveness in higher education: Changes in the entry requirements and the approval process of equity measures for disadvantaged students in Hungary Abstract This study examines how Hungarian Higher Education (HE) admission policies from 2007 to 2023 affected access for applicants with Socioeconomic Disadvantages (SED) and Cumulative Social Disadvantages (CSD). It assesses the impact of legal and administrative changes on the number, proportion, and admission success of these groups. The research is grounded in international and national literature on higher education inclusion that emphasizes access being a critical point in the process of inclusion. In Hungary, a system of centrally regulated equity measures is one of the few mechanisms that can compensate for structural inequalities, but even these positive actions were significantly restricted after 2013. Moreover, these policy shifts occurred within an education system where social background strongly influences students' trajectories, making equitable admission practices even more relevant. Our research uses document analysis of legislation and admission guidelines, supplemented by time-series statistical analysis of national application and enrollment data supported by KIR-STAT datasets. title: Educational functions of Uşak tales in the context of functional theory
text_snippet: Educational functions of Uşak tales in the context of functional theory Abstract Folk tales are ancient traces that shape the cultural identities of societies. Passed down orally from generation to generation, folk tales have significant functions both in the transmission of culture and in education. By fostering children's imagination, folk tales serve as a bridge from their limitless imaginary worlds to real life. Supported in their cognitive development, children are able to navigate more effectively between fiction and reality through folk tales. Additionally, folk tales help children perceive a just world order where bad behaviors are punished and good behaviors rewarded. Holding an important place within Turkish culture, folk tales contribute not only to educational development but also to raising awareness of national and universal cultural values among children. Like many other folklore products, folk tales serve various functions in production and transmission. Among these, William Bascom categorizes folklore's functions into four main types: entertainment, reinforcement of values, transmission of education, and escapism from oppression. title: Effects of ChatGPT-flipped instruction on the academic performance and self-regulated skill of L2 pre-service teachers in Ondo State, Nigeria
text_snippet: Effects of ChatGPT-flipped instruction on the academic performance and self-regulated skill of L2 pre-service teachers in Ondo State, Nigeria Abstract Concerns have been raised by scholars over unethical use of ChatGPT in academic settings. While some institutions have condemned or even banned its use, integrating it into classroom instruction could help mitigate these unethical practices. One effective approach is ChatGPT-Flipped Instruction. This study examines the effects of ChatGPT-Flipped Instruction on the Academic Performance and Self-regulated Skills of L2 Pre-Service Teachers at Adekunle Ajasin University, Ondo state, Nigeria. A quasi-experimental research design was adopted with subjects randomly assigned to the experimental groups ( n = 150) which received varying levels of ChatGPT exposure across six instructional phases and the control group ( n = 150). The research instruments were the English for Specific Purposes Test (ESPT, r = 0.81) and the Self-Regulation Skills Questionnaire (SSSQ, r = 0.76). Among other findings, the results revealed that ChatGPT-Flipped Instruction had a more significant relative effect on students' performance with a mean post-test score of M = 89.94 (SD = 3.04) compared to M = 69.99 (SD = 3.04) for students taught using traditional methods. title: Navigating diversity: Teacher attitudes towards multicultural education in Türkiye Post-Syrian War
text_snippet: Navigating diversity: Teacher attitudes towards multicultural education in Türkiye Post-Syrian War Abstract This study aims to systematically examine teacher attitudes toward multicultural education in Türkiye between 2000 and 2024, with a specific focus on the impact of the Syrian Civil War. It seeks to understand how socio-political changes have shaped educators' perspectives and practices regarding cultural diversity in classrooms. The research builds on the premise that multicultural education has gained increased relevance in Türkiye, particularly due to the influx of Syrian refugee students. However, institutional responses and teacher preparedness remain inconsistent across regions. Using the PRISMA framework, 56 empirical, peer-reviewed studies were selected from 1,035 records screened across Google Scholar, EBSCO, and Dergipark. Studies were included if they focused on Türkiye and addressed teacher attitudes or experiences with multicultural education. Findings indicate a dominance of quantitative methods (65.5%), with fewer qualitative (24.1%) and mixed-methods (6.9%) studies. title: Teaching English in rural Vietnam: How EFL teachers define themselves?
text_snippet: Teaching English in rural Vietnam: How EFL teachers define themselves? Abstract Rural areas in Vietnam often face challenges such as limited resources, lower levels of English proficiency among students, and fewer professional development opportunities for teachers, making the role of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) educators in these regions both vital and demanding. This study explores the professional identities of K-12 EFL teachers in rural areas of Vietnam. Using a qualitative approach and drawing on Conceptual Metaphor Theory, data were collected through metaphor elicitation from 24 EFL teachers currently working in rural Vietnam. Metaphor analysis was employed to analyse the collected metaphors. The study highlights how participants perceive and construct their professional identities within the unique socio-cultural and educational challenges of rural contexts. Six umbrella metaphors emerged as central to their experiences: teacher as a motivator, a ferry, a cultural ambassador, a seed sower, a juggler in a circus, and a home. This research adds to a deeper understanding of rural EFL teachers’ identities, providing insights for educators and policymakers to improve teacher retention and support systems in underserved regions.

title: Reducing general foreign language classroom anxiety through flipped instruction: An experimental study in EFL contexts
text_snippet: Reducing general foreign language classroom anxiety through flipped instruction: An experimental study in EFL contexts Abstract The main aim of the present research was to examine the potential of flipped classroom teaching in reducing general foreign language classroom anxiety (FLCAS) among first-year EFL students in Algeria. It also aimed to explore the moderating roles of gender and learner motivation in the impacts of flipped teaching. While flipped classrooms have been increasingly popular in terms of facilitating learners' engagement and reducing anxiety, empirical studies on their differential impact based on gender and motivation type are quite limited. A pre-test–post-test quasi-experimental control group design was employed with 120 undergraduate EFL students at Nour Bachir University Center, stratified by gender and level of language proficiency. Students were assigned to a flipped or traditional instruction group and multivariate analyses were conducted. Mixed-design ANOVA showed significantly greater anxiety reductions for the flipped group, particularly for integratively motivated and female students. title: A systematic review on teacher resilience assessment: Trends, foci, and implications
text_snippet: A systematic review on teacher resilience assessment: Trends, foci, and implications Abstract Teacher resilience (TR) has gained increasing attention as a key factor in teacher well-being, career retention, and adaptive professional practice. Despite rapid growth in the broader TR literature, limited attention has been given to how resilience is assessed, how methodological choices shape what is measured, and how assessment findings relate to professional outcomes. This systematic review synthesizes empirical research on Teacher Resilience Assessment (TRA) published between 2010 and 2022, drawing on 52 studies identified through a PRISMA-guided search. The review maps publication patterns, geographic distribution, and methodological designs and provides a thematic synthesis of key conceptual foci in TRA research. Five interconnected domains are identified: personal and psychological resilience, emotional regulation and coping, professional commitment and adaptive practice, relational and organizational supports, and contextual and crisis-related influences. title: Attitudes of elementary school teachers towards environmental education: A comparative survey from Slovak and Hungarian schools
text_snippet: Attitudes of elementary school teachers towards environmental education: A comparative survey from Slovak and Hungarian schools Abstract This study aimed to examine primary school teachers' attitudes toward environmental education (EE) in schools with Slovak and Hungarian as the language of instruction in Slovakia. Understanding how language of instruction and contextual factors influence EE practices is vital in multilingual education systems. Previous research highlights the role of teacher engagement, thematic diversity, and access to resources in shaping EE attitudes. However, limited attention has been given to linguistic inequalities within the Slovak educational context. Using a cross-sectional quantitative design ( N = 83), we applied Kruskal-Wallis tests and Spearman's correlation analysis to explore the effects of demographic and contextual variables. Demographic factors such as age and gender showed no significant influence, while teaching experience, frequency of EE implementation, and topic diversity significantly predicted attitudes. Slovak-speaking teachers reported greater access to EE resources ( p = 0.00001), broader topic coverage ( p = 0.0279), and more positive overall attitudes ( p = 0.0310). title: Exploring educative teaching for Bildung - A non-affirmative approach to Didaktik for schools
text_snippet: Exploring educative teaching for Bildung - A non-affirmative approach to Didaktik for schools Abstract As a response to the pedagogical paradoxes of subjectivity and intersubjectivity, this article proposes non-affirmative school didactic theory as a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding educative teaching for Bildung in the context of comprehensive education. This approach conceptualizes curriculum work, teaching, leadership, and assessment as distributed, relational, and multi-level phenomena. The argument put forth is that education in political democracies requires both policies and practices that align with the principles of non-affirmative emancipation—principles that go beyond mere transmission of knowledge or socialization into predefined norms. Non-affirmative school didactics builds upon classical educational concepts developed within European modern educational thought, such as Bildsamkeit (the capacity for self-formation), the summons to self-activity, and recognition, as formulated by scholars like Dietrich Benner. It also draws on Herbart's notion of educative teaching, which sees teaching as more than instruction—it is a moral and reflective practice that fosters autonomous and responsible individuals. title: Addressing the unknown learner: Non-affirmative theory of education and pedagogical challenges of recognition
text_snippet: Addressing the unknown learner: Non-affirmative theory of education and pedagogical challenges of recognition Abstract The study aims at describing the role of recognition in education theory. Its starting point is the meaning and relevance of recognition in NAT (non-affirmative theory of education and Bildung). While NAT widely refers to classical modern approaches, two directions of present recognition theory are investigated to problematize NAT's triadic interrelation of summoning to self-activity, recognition and Bildsamkeit. With regard to Honneth the dependency of children on their summoning teachers and educators can be described to characterize autonomization in relations of power and struggle. The focus on manifold practices of recognition leads to approaches of subjectivation theory that shed light on ambivalences in addressing the Other as a certain Other without being able to know the Other. Thus, NAT's differentiation between affirmative recognition and non-affirmative summoning to self-activity can be irritated by a relationality that goes beyond clear separations to explore manifold forms of pedagogical tact that takes care of the single and social determined learner who is free and determined at once.

title: Family additional language policy and planning in Hungary
text_snippet: Family additional language policy and planning in Hungary Abstract This article connects two fields of applied linguistics: research into the role of the social context in learning additional languages and Language Policy and Planning. It introduces Family Additional Language Policy and Planning as an approach to analysing parental role in children's additional language learning. We applied Family Additional Language Policy and Planning in empirical research, and through conducting and analysing interviews with 28 Hungarian parents whose children attended schools with a pupil composition of lower-than-average socioeconomic status, found that they exercised conscious and overt Family Additional Language Policy and Planning, which can be labelled as ‘maximising options’, aiming to provide their children with symbolic linguistic capital parents might not possess and that can be converted to economic, social, and cultural capital parents lack. title: Being a member of the community: Participation and inclusion of international students in higher education
text_snippet: Being a member of the community: Participation and inclusion of international students in higher education Abstract International student numbers are growing globally, yet their inclusion and engagement within university communities remain underexplored. Existing research highlights the importance of international students' participation in extracurricular activities (ECAs) and student government organisations (SGOs) in fostering inclusion and belonging. However, gaps persist in understanding how cultural and systemic barriers impact their experiences. This study focuses on international students at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Hungary, addressing these gaps by examining their participation in ECAs and SGOs and identifying factors influencing their engagement. Using a quantitative methodology, data from 77 international students were collected via a structured questionnaire. Analysis revealed significant challenges, including language barriers, limited awareness of SGOs, and disparities in engagement opportunities compared to local students. While over 50% of respondents reported recent participation in ECAs, their involvement in SGOs was minimal. title: Preservice physical education teacher's self-efficacy: A cross-cultural comparative study in Türkiye and Hungary
text_snippet: Preservice physical education teacher's self-efficacy: A cross-cultural comparative study in Türkiye and Hungary Abstract This study aimed to determine the teaching self-efficacy of Hungarian and Turkish preservice physical education teachers (PrePETs) and to identify the similarities and differences between two countries with different educational systems in the context of demographic factors. Research indicates that self-efficacy (SE) is critical to preservice teachers' ability to cope with challenges, their professional development, and effective performance and teaching practices. Although there is numerous research on SE, studies on PrePETs remain under-represented, especially in cross-national studies. Therefore, a cross-sectional survey design was employed involving o 107 Hungarian and Turkish PrePET. Data were collected using the Teacher Self-Efficacy Scale and the Demographic Questionnaire. The results revealed that both Turkish and Hungarian PrePETs showed higher SE with no significant differences observed based on gender, GPA, age, or country. However, teaching experience was a statistically differentiating factor while it has a positive, modest correlation with Turkish candidates, it had a negative, weak correlation among Hungarian candidates. title: Reinterpreting the pedagogy of care through non-affirmative theory in the era of neoliberal education
text_snippet: Reinterpreting the pedagogy of care through non-affirmative theory in the era of neoliberal education Abstract Increasing evidence suggests a global shift in education towards market-driven policy has eroded fundamental human virtues including relationships, empathy, responsiveness, and important of collective practices, resulting in a moral crisis of care that affects students, teachers, and families. This shift has led to what Butler terms moral precarity, raising concerns that younger generation may lose their sense of responsibility and commitment to care for others. Drawing on existing literature, this paper suggests that the ethics of care with its relational ontology and maternal epistemology provides a robust ethical framework to address these challenges. However, critics argue that care ethics may inadvertently neglect respect for autonomy, creating a tension between relational interdependence and individual autonomy. title: A comparative study of Educational Subject Philosophy in China and non-affirmative theory of education
text_snippet: A comparative study of Educational Subject Philosophy in China and non-affirmative theory of education Abstract Under neoliberalism, instrumentalization of education for economic purposes has been intensely accentuated in post-industrial societies, necessitating critical reflection on both educational practice and theory. How should a theory of education be structured as to consider both societal needs and the individual's right to develop as a cultural subject and political citizen? Non-Affirmative Theory of Education (NAT) and Educational Subject Philosophy (ESP) represent theoretical attempts to address the question in Europe and China. This study undertakes a comparative analysis of the two approaches that seek to respond to the same educational problem from different perspectives. The comparative analysis reveals that ESP conceptualizes the nature of education as subjectivity and NAT as non-affirmativity . Both approaches emphasize education as a specialized activity aimed at cultivating individuals, advocating for the development of culturally reflective and self-determining subjects.
